findings: Arnold combines verses 1.26 and 1.27 into a single unified sentence describing relatives across both armies, accurately represented as a shared source span.

Verse 1.43 is a genuine source omission flagged by Arnold in footnote 1 ("Some repetitionary lines are here omitted"), and 1.44 preserves only the closing clause "So teach our holy hymns" (ityanuśuśruma).
Arnold translation in 1.10 renders aparyāptam as "Weakest" and paryāptam as "something too strong", reflecting his poetic translation choice rather than an alignment fault.

Arnold varies meter across Chapter 2: rhyming quatrains for Arjuna despondency (2.5-2.8), dactylic hexameters for the immortal Spirit (2.20), rhyming lyric stanzas for 2.22, 2.29, and 2.70, and blank verse for the philosophical dialogues.
All 72 canonical verses are represented one-to-one with excellent semantic fidelity and complete source coverage.
Chapter 3 maintains exact verse-by-verse alignment for all 43 canonical references without any textual gaps, omissions, or shared ranges.
The sacrificial cycle (yajña, Prajapati, rain, food in 3.10-3.16) and the psychological escalation of desire (3.36-3.43) map cleanly to their respective Sanskrit shlokas.
Chapter 4 provides unbroken, one-to-one alignment for all 42 canonical references without omissions, expansions, or text loss.
The avatar declaration (4.7-4.8) and the comprehensive categorization of yajñas (4.24-4.32) are accurately segmented.
Twenty intra-line verse transitions (e.g. 4.1/4.2, 4.5-4.8, 4.10-4.13, 4.17-4.23, 4.25/4.26, 4.32-4.37, 4.39-4.42) reflect precise poetic clause divisions.

Arnold tightly intertwines the difficulty of renunciation (5.6) and the qualities of the yogayukta (5.7) into a single period ("Yet such abstraction, Chief! Is hard to win without much holiness... A Yogayukt--he is a Saint who wends Straightway to Brahm. Such an one is not touched By taint of deeds"), accurately mapped as a shared source span.
Verses 5.8 and 5.9 divide the sensory activities catalogue cleanly between 5.8 ("seeing, hearing... slumbers") and 5.9 ("or talks, Holds fast...") across line 999.
Verse 5.17 preserves Arnold bracketed poetic gloss "[Who will may have this Light; Who hath it sees.]" alongside the translation.
All 29 canonical references are fully accounted for with complete source span coverage.
Chapter 6 exhibits complete, verse-by-verse one-to-one fidelity for all 47 canonical references.
The practical meditation instructions (6.10-6.15), the four-verse definition of Yoga (6.20-6.23), and the destiny of the fallen seeker (6.37-6.45) align seamlessly with their Sanskrit counterparts.
Chapter 7 translation exhibits complete 1-to-1 canonical coverage with no omissions or merged shlokas.

Mid-line poetic divisions (notably verses 7.8/7.9, 7.9/7.10, 7.10/7.11, 7.11/7.12, 7.12/7.13, 7.13/7.14, 7.20/7.21, 7.23/7.24, 7.26/7.27, 7.27/7.28) have been cleanly partitioned at syntactic and semantic boundaries.
Translator notes FN#12, FN#13, and FN#14 are accurately positioned on their respective canonical references.
Verses 8.23 through 8.27 constitute a genuine five-verse source omission spanning ten Sanskrit hemistichs, correctly marked in the alignment with empty content and an explanatory note.
The source text anomaly wherein Gutenberg edition prints [FN#14] at the omission ellipsis instead of [FN#15] is faithfully noted without modifying the source text or corrupting the alignment.
Verses 8.9 and 8.10 are rendered in distinct four-line poetic stanzas with alternating rhyme, accurately corresponding to the respective canonical shlokas.
Chapter 9 contains a complete 1-to-1 verse translation for all 34 canonical verses without omissions or multi-verse consolidations.
The poetic transitions across metrical shifts (such as the rhymed stanzas in verses 9.20 and 9.21) maintain strict semantic alignment with the underlying Sanskrit text.

Chapter 10 contains 42 canonical references; verses 10.4 and 10.5 form a verified shared two-verse span where Arnold combines their list of mental dispositions and attributes into an 8-line rhymed catalogue.
The source footnote marker anomaly [FN#l6] (using lowercase 'l' for digit 1) is faithfully preserved at verse 10.1 without affecting the text integrity.
The heptameter rhyming couplets adopted by Arnold from verse 10.1 onwards adhere closely to the semantic progression of the Sanskrit vibhūti enumerations.

Chapter 11 contains 55 canonical verses; verses 11.26 and 11.27 form a verified shared two-verse span where Arnold combines the naming of the warriors with their horrifying destruction in the cosmic jaws.
The chapter transitions across multiple lyric metrical forms (including rhymed stanzas for Sanjaya's description and Arjuna's awe-filled hymn) without losing semantic fidelity or verse boundaries.
Footnotes [FN#21], [FN#22], [FN#23], and [FN#24] are properly preserved and positioned.
Chapter 12 translation provides complete 1-to-1 canonical coverage across all 20 verses without omissions or mergers.
Arnold structures the concluding portrait of the ideal devotee with the recurring cadence 'That man I love!', faithfully reflecting the repeated Sanskrit refrain 'sa me priyaḥ'.
Footnote [FN#25] is accurately positioned on the translation of 'anapeksha' in verse 12.16.

Canonical 13.1 begins with Krishna's discourse; Arjuna's introductory three lines ('Now would I hear...') are correctly segregated as recensional prelude paratext in accordance with the standard 34-verse canon.
Verse 13.4 is an explicit, verified source omission; Arnold omitted the two Sanskrit lines referencing Vedic chants and Brahma-sutra reasoning with an ellipsis and footnote 28.
Verses 13.9, 13.10, and 13.11 feature clean intra-line boundary splits around 'with a will set firm' and 'endeavours resolute', preserving exact semantic verse correspondences without bleed.
All 34 canonical references are fully accounted for with high semantic fidelity.
Complete 27-verse coverage with zero omissions or verse-merging.
Precise intra-line splits at verse boundaries: line 42 cleanly divides 14.12 ('engrained;') and 14.13 ('and where'), and line 95 divides 14.24 ('dispraise;') and 14.25 ('satisfied').
Arnold renders technical Guna terminology with poetic Victorian archaisms ('Soothfastness', 'Passion', 'Ignorance') while preserving exact philosophical distinctions.
Arnold translates verses 15.1–15.6 in lyrical rhymed stanzas ('Parable of the fig-tree', note 30), requiring careful inter-stanza clause alignment across enjambments.
Verse 15.15 is an explicit, verified source omission where Arnold dropped the shloka on memory, knowledge, and Vedic authorship, directly attested by footnote 31.
The remaining 19 verses map with exceptional precision to canonical 15.1–15.14 and 15.16–15.20.

Translator footnote 33 asserts the omission of 'the ten concluding shlokas, with Mr Davis', whereas standard canonical Chapter 16 has 24 verses total, leaving exactly two omitted shlokas (16.23–16.24); this discrepancy is a historical source anomaly correctly preserved.
The divine virtues catalog in 16.1–16.3 is split with exceptional accuracy across line boundaries (line 6 at 'Uprightness,' and line 13 at 'manhood nobly mixed').
Careful segmentation of demonic psychological profiles across verses 16.10–16.11, 16.15–16.16, and 16.19–16.20 accurately reflects the Sanskrit syntactic units.

Arnold deliberately terminates his translation after verse 17.22 (the three kinds of gifts), omitting canonical 17.23–17.28 with explicit translator note 37 ('I omit the concluding shlokas, as of very doubtful authenticity').
All 6 concluding verses (17.23 through 17.28) are verified as legitimate source omissions, faithfully aligned without artificial filler text.
Verses 17.5 and 17.6 split the description of unscriptural austerities and bodily self-torture cleanly across verse boundaries.

Witness data anomaly identified: in verse 18.45, the input witness record mistakenly embeds the text of 5.10 ('He who does actions, offering them to Brahman...'), but Arnold's translation ('Whoso performeth--diligent, content-- / The work allotted him...') is verified as a direct and accurate rendering of canonical 18.45.

Complex poetic metre transitions in 18.67–18.71 (rhymed heptameter couplets for the phala-shruti) and 18.74–18.78 (long-line hymnic verse for Sanjaya's closing vision) are partitioned with high precision across verse boundaries.
Intra-line verse cuts in 18.36/18.37, 18.69/18.70, and 18.76/18.77/18.78 are verified to exact character boundaries, ensuring zero missing or duplicated lines across all 78 verses.

reviews.notes: Dhritarashtra opening question to Sanjaya on the holy field of Kurukshetra is cleanly translated, preserving speaker prefix.
Sanjaya opening narrative as Duryodhana approaches Drona upon seeing the Pandava army arrayed.
Duryodhana address to Drona pointing out the Pandava battle array marshaled by Drupada son.
Catalog of heroic Pandava bowmen comparable to Bhima and Arjuna (Virata, Yuyudhana, Drupada).
Enumeration of Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, King of Kasi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Saibya.
Enumeration of Yudhamanyu, Uttamaujas, Saubhadra (Abhimanyu), and Draupadi sons.
Duryodhana turns to recount the principal commanders on his own side to the preceptor Drona.
Listing of Kaurava leaders: Drona, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Vikarna, Asvatthaman, and Saumadatti.
Reference to countless other valiant warriors ready to lay down their lives for Duryodhana.

Order to all Kaurava divisions to guard Bhishma steadfastly.
Bhishma blowing the great conch with a lion-like roar to gladden Duryodhana.
Sudden clamor of Kaurava horns, drums, tabors, and cymbals sounding like a tempest.
Krishna and Arjuna seen on their magnificent golden chariot yoked with white steeds.
Blowing of divine conches: Krishna blowing Panchajanya, Arjuna blowing Devadatta, Bhima blowing Paundra.
Yudhishthira blowing Anantavijaya, Nakula blowing Sughosha, and Sahadeva blowing Manipushpaka.
Kasi prince, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and unconquered Satyaki blowing conches.
Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and Saubhadra blowing their battle shells all together.
The tumultuous roar piercing the hearts of the Kauravas and echoing across earth and heaven.
Arjuna, bearing the monkey banner (Hanuman), beholding the battle set and lifting his bow to speak to Krishna.
Arjuna request to Krishna to station the chariot between the two opposing hosts.
Arjuna desire to scrutinize those standing arrayed and eager for combat.
Arjuna observing those bent on battle to please the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra.
Sanjaya narration of Krishna driving the chariot into the space between the two hosts.
Krishna halting the chariot before Bhishma and Drona and bidding Arjuna behold the assembled Kurus.
Arjuna surveying grandfathers, fathers, teachers, uncles, and kinsmen; unified with 1.27 in shared source span.
Survey of kinsmen on both sides; shared span with 1.26 properly absorbs introductory transitional clause ending at 1.27.
Arjuna direct speech lamenting the sight of assembled kinsmen gathered for mutual slaughter.
Somatic symptoms of dejection: failing limbs, parched mouth, bodily trembling, and horripilation.
Gandiva slipping from the hand, burning sensation of skin, and spinning of the mind.
Arjuna perceiving adverse omens and seeing no good arising from slaying kinsmen in battle.
Renunciation of desire for victory, sovereignty, and pleasures purchased by kinsmen blood.
Arjuna highlighting that those for whose sake royal life is coveted now stand ready to die.
Enumeration of teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, uncles, and fathers-in-law.
Refusal to slay kinsmen even for sovereignty over the three worlds, much less the earthly realm.
Reflection on sin and sorrow that would ensue from killing the Dhartarashtras.
Conclusion that it is improper to slay kinsmen, as no happiness can come from destroying one own people.
Acknowledgment that opponents are blinded by greed (lobhopahata-cetasaḥ) to the guilt of family ruin.
Arjuna urging that those who clearly discern the sin of destroying family lines must turn away from it.
Doctrinal explanation of family destruction leading to the collapse of eternal family dharmas.
Ascendance of adharma causing corruption of women and consequent caste confusion (varna-samkara).
Ancestors falling from heaven bereft of funeral cakes and libations; note [FN#1] marks omission of repetitive lines.
Verified source omission: Arnold omitted Sanskrit 1.43 under footnote 1 ("Some repetitionary lines are here omitted").
Arnold "So teach our holy hymns" translates the closing clause ityanuśuśruma, with the rest of 1.44 omitted alongside 1.43.
Lamentation over undertaking great sin through greed for kingdom pleasures (Ahovat! = aho bata).
Arjuna preference to be slain weaponless and unresisting by armed Kauravas.
Sanjaya closing narrative: Arjuna casting away bow and arrows and sinking despondent on chariot seat.
Sanjaya opening narrative describing Arjuna overcome by compassion and tearful dejection.
Krishna rebuke of Arjuna sudden faint-heartedness and ignoble dejection on the verge of battle.
Krishna summons Arjuna to discard unmanly weakness (klaibyam) and arise as scourge of foes.
Arjuna protests against shooting arrows at revered elders Bhishma and Drona worthy of honor.
Arjuna reflects that living on beggar bread is preferable to tasting blood-tainted feasts of victory (lyrical meter).
Uncertainty as to whether victory or defeat is preferable when killing kinsmen drains life of purpose.
Arjuna confession of spiritual distress (kārpaṇya-doṣa) and formal surrender to Krishna as his disciple.
Arjuna despairing admission that unchallenged earthly dominion or divine sovereignty cannot heal his grief.
Sanjaya relates Arjuna declaring "I will not fight" to Govinda before falling silent.
Krishna, gently smiling between the opposing armies, begins his divine instruction to grieving Arjuna.
Opening instruction: the wise mourn neither for the living nor the dead (aśocyān anvaśocas tvam).
Affirmation of eternal existence: Krishna, Arjuna, and all kings have never not existed nor will ever cease to be.
Analogy of the embodied soul traversing childhood, youth, and old age before passing into another frame.
Sense-contacts generating fleeting experiences of heat, cold, pleasure, and pain to be endured patiently.
The steadfast soul undisturbed by sensory dualities (sama-duḥkha-sukha) is fit for immortality.
The ontological doctrine of sat and asat: the unreal has no being, the real never ceases to be.
The imperishable nature of the all-pervading Spirit which none can destroy.
Finite bodies perish while the embodied indweller remains eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable.
Ignorance of those who believe the soul slays or is slain; Spirit neither slays nor can be slain.
Celebrated declaration of the soul birthless, deathless, changeless nature rendered in dactylic hexameters.
He who realizes the Soul as unborn and undecaying understands that nobody slays or causes to be slain.
The classic metaphor of casting off outworn garments to put on new robes as the soul adopts new frames.
Weapons cleave it not, fire burns it not, water wets it not, and wind withers it not.
Soul characterized as impenetrable, incombustible, unassailable, all-pervading, stable, and eternal.
Unmanifest, unthinkable, immutable soul: knowing this truth leaves no ground for lamentation.
Argument a fortiori: even if the soul were held to experience constant birth and death, grief is misplaced.
Ineluctability of cosmic cycle: death is certain for the born, and birth certain for the dead.
Beings are unmanifest in origin, manifest in the middle state, and unmanifest again in dissolution.
Contemplation of the wonder (āścaryavat) of the Soul, which remains uncomprehended even after hearing.
The indwelling Self in all bodies is perpetually invulnerable; therefore mourn no living creature.
Appeal to Kshatriya svadharma: no higher duty exists for a warrior than a lawful, righteous fight.
Unsolicited righteous war described as an open portal to heaven for fortunate warriors.
Warning that refusing this righteous battle means abandoning svadharma and fame, thereby incurring sin.
Infamy and loss of honor will be proclaimed perpetually, which is far worse than physical death.
Great car-warriors (mahārathāḥ) will ascribe withdrawal to fear, turning former esteem into contempt.
Enemies will voice abusive and slanderous words mocking warrior prowess, causing supreme distress.
Binary warrior outcome: slain one wins heaven, victorious one rules earth; arise resolute for battle.
Equanimity in pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat: fighting thus incurs no sin.
Transition from Sankhya theory to Yoga practice (Buddhi-yoga), through which action-bonds are severed.
No effort is wasted in Buddhi-yoga, no contrary outcome occurs, and a little of this virtue saves from great fear.
Single-pointed resolute intellect (vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ) contrasted with multi-branched irresolution.
Critique of flowery Vedic rhetoric extolled by those lacking discernment who say nothing else matters.
Sensory-bound ritualists craving heaven, prescribing diverse ceremonies yielding wealth and rebirth.
Those attached to power and pleasure whose minds are carried away lack steady meditative resolution.
Exhortation to transcend the three gunas of the Vedas, beyond dualities, established in pure being; notes [FN#2, FN#3].
Analogy of all the Vedas being to the enlightened seer what a small water tank is amidst an all-pervading flood.
Cardinal dictum of karma yoga: right to the action alone, never to its fruit; shun inaction.
Equanimity in success and failure defined as Yoga: perform duties established in holy detachment.
Mere ritual action is far inferior to Buddhi-yoga; pity upon those motivated by fruit of deeds.
The wise yoked in equanimity cast off good and evil deeds alike; yoga is excellence in action.
Sages relinquishing fruits of action are freed from the bond of rebirth, mounting to the painless seat.
When intellect clears the forest of delusion, high indifference is attained toward heard and unread doctrine.
When intellect, perplexed by diverse theological texts, rests unswerving in samadhi, Yoga is won.
Arjuna inquires concerning the characteristics of the person of steady wisdom (sthita-prajña).
Krishna defines sthita-prajña as one who sheds all mental desires, satisfied in the Self alone by the Self.
Unhappiness does not deject him, joy does not elate him; he is free from passion, fear, and wrath (muni).
Unattached in all things, welcoming neither good nor evil with joy or hatred, his wisdom is steadfast.
Sensory withdrawal likened to the tortoise drawing its limbs securely into its protective shell.
Abstinence drops sense-objects but leaves subtle longing; even longing vanishes upon beholding the Supreme.
The turbulent senses can violently sweep away even the mind of a wise person earnestly striving.
Subduing all senses, intent upon Me; wisdom is firmly seated in him whose senses are thoroughly mastered.
Causal cascade of downfall: brooding on sense-objects leads to attachment, desire, and flare of wrath.
Anger breeds delusion, delusion causes loss of memory, memory-loss ruins intellect, ending in total ruin.
Moving among sense-objects with senses self-controlled and free from attraction and revulsion yields serenity.
Serenity brings cessation of all earthly sorrows; the intellect of the tranquil soon becomes firmly anchored.
The undisciplined has neither wisdom nor meditation; without meditation there is no peace, without peace no joy.
A mind wandering after roving senses sweeps away wisdom, just as a gale sweeps a vessel across the waters.
Wisdom is firmly established in him whose senses are wholly curbed from their corresponding objects.
What is night to all creatures is the wakeful state of the disciplined sage; the world day is his night.
Ocean metaphor: as rivers enter the full ocean without swelling it, desires enter the sage without disturbing his peace.
Renouncing all cravings, devoid of longing, egotism, and possessiveness, one attains utter peace.
The state of Brahman (brāhmī sthitiḥ): attaining it, one is not deluded; abiding therein at death, one enters Brahma-nirvana.
Arjuna opening dilemma: if knowledge is ranked above action, why urge participation in terrible warfare?
Arjuna asks Krishna to resolve seemingly conflicting counsel and clearly indicate the single path to supreme good.
Krishna sets forth the twofold spiritual path: contemplation for the Sankhyas and action for the Yogins.
Abstaining from action does not secure freedom from action (naiṣkarmyam), nor does mere renunciation bring perfection.
No living being remains motionless even for an instant, compelled to act by the innate gunas of Nature.
Denunciation of the hypocrite who reins in outer physical organs while mentally indulging in sensory objects.
Praise of the earnest seeker who governs the senses with the mind and undertakes karma-yoga unattached.
Injunction to perform allotted duties: work is superior to idleness, and bodily life itself requires action.
Work performed as sacred offering (yajñārthāt karmaṇaḥ) frees from worldly bondage; act selflessly for sacrifice.
Cosmic institution: Prajapati creating mankind alongside sacrifice, calling it the wish-yielding cow (Kamaduk).
Reciprocal obligation: foster the divine powers through sacrifice that they in turn may foster human life.
Gods reward selfless labor; one who consumes divine bounties without offering sacrificial return is a thief.
Righteous eaters of sacrificial remnants are absolved of fault, while those cooking solely for themselves eat sin.
Cosmic chain: beings live by food, food comes from rain, rain from sacrifice, and sacrifice from human action.
Action originates in Brahma, and Brahma from the Imperishable; the all-pervading divine is rooted in sacrifice.
Censure of one who refuses to sustain this cosmic wheel, indulging sensual appetite in vain, sinful existence.
Exemption for the self-realized sage who delights in the Self, satisfied and contented in the Self alone.
For the enlightened sage there is nothing to gain by action or inaction, and no dependency on creatures; note [FN#5].
Admonition to perform prescribed tasks with detachment, as selfless action conducts man to highest liberation.
Historical exemplar: King Janaka and ancient seers attained perfection through duty and world-maintenance (loka-saṅgraham).
Leadership principle: whatever standards eminent men set, ordinary people adopt and follow.
Krishna personal example: possessing no unfulfilled desires across the three worlds, yet ever engaged in action.
If the Lord ceased tireless action, mankind would follow that idle example and decline into degradation.
Cosmic ruin and confusion of human order would result if divine sustenance through righteous action were withdrawn.
The enlightened should work without attachment for the welfare of the world, just as the ignorant work for personal ends.
The wise must not unsettle the minds of the unenlightened, but inspire them by dedicated engagement in all duties.
All activities are operated by the qualities of Nature; the egoist deceived by self-conceit thinks "I am the doer".
The seer of truth recognizes that gunas act upon gunas, standing detached and unentangled in acts.
Those blinded by Nature qualities remain attached to works; the person of complete vision must not perturb them.
Command to dedicate all works to Krishna with spiritual focus, devoid of selfish hope or egoism, fighting free of fever.
Liberation promised to those who faithfully and without carping practice this divine doctrine in daily conduct.
Those who revile and ignore this ordinance are declared devoid of wisdom, senseless, and doomed to spiritual ruin.
Even the learned follow their innate disposition; all beings conform to nature, and mere suppression is futile.
Sensory organs have instinctive likes and dislikes toward their objects; one must not be enslaved by these twin adversaries.
Superiority of one own duty (svadharma) over an alien path: death in one own calling is blessed, another path is fraught with dread.
Arjuna inquires what mysterious force compels a man to commit sinful deeds as if dragged against his will.
Krishna identifies desire (kāma) and anger (krodha), springing from the rajas quality, as humanity voracious enemy.
Tripartite simile of desire obscuring truth: like smoke enveloping flame, rust/dust a mirror, and the womb the embryo.
Wisdom is veiled by this eternal adversary of the wise, assuming the protean and insatiable shape of desire.
The senses, mind, and intellect are identified as the fortress and stronghold of desire whence it bewilders the soul.
Injunction to master the senses at the outset and destroy this sinful destroyer of knowledge and spiritual discernment.
Psychological hierarchy: senses are subtle, mind is higher than senses, intellect higher than mind, and the Soul above intellect.
Concluding charge: perceiving the Supreme Self beyond intellect, subdue lower self by the Self and slay desire.
Krishna recounts primordial transmission of Yoga to Vivasvan (Sun god), then Manu, then Ikshvaku.
Transmission through royal sages (rājarṣayaḥ) and subsequent decay of the ancient lineage over time.
Krishna reveals this supreme secret Yoga anew to Arjuna because he is a loyal devotee and beloved friend.
Arjuna chronological question: how could Krishna have taught Vivasvan who lived ages earlier in time?
Krishna explains the reality of multiple births: I remember them all, whereas thou rememberest them not.
Divine incarnation doctrine: unborn, imperishable Lord taking birth through his own creative power (Maya).
Celebrated avatar declaration: whenever righteousness declines and evil rises, I manifest Myself.
Purpose of divine descent: protecting the virtuous, destroying evildoers, and restoring dharma age after age.
Whoso comprehends the truth of Krishna divine birth and work transcends rebirth, merging into His being.
Many seekers, purified by the austerity of wisdom and freed from passion, fear, and wrath, attain divine union.
Universal responsiveness: in whatever way men approach Me, so do I welcome them; all paths lead to Me.
Men worship lesser deities seeking swift worldly fruit, which readily materializes in this mortal realm.
Creation of the four orders (cāturvarṇyam) based on innate qualities and duties; God is author yet non-doer.
Works do not contaminate the Lord because He harbors no craving for fruits; knowing this frees from karmic bondage.
Ancient seekers after liberation acted with this understanding; Arjuna is urged to follow their venerable footsteps.
The paradox of action and inaction that confuses even sages; Krishna promises to expound saving knowledge.
Necessity to distinguish lawful action, prohibited action (vikarma), and inaction (akarma); deep is the path.
Highest insight: he who discerns inaction in action, and action in inaction, is truly wise among humans.
The sage whose enterprises are devoid of selfish intent has his works consumed in the fire of wisdom.
Renouncing fruit of action, ever content, and independent, one remains inactive in spirit even while acting.
Free from yearning, self-controlled, relinquishing greed, performing mere bodily functions without guilt.
Content with whatever chance brings, transcending dualities, free from envy, equal in success and failure.
The work of an unattached, liberated soul whose consciousness is anchored in wisdom melts away wholly.
All is Brahman: the ladle, the oblation, the fire, the offerer, and the goal of him who meditates on Brahman.
Survey of sacrifices: some offer worship to the gods; others offer sacrifice into the flame of Brahman.
Ascetics who offer the senses into the fire of restraint, and others who offer sense-objects into sense-fires.
Yogins offering all vital and sensory actions into the fire of self-discipline kindled by wisdom.
Variety of seekers: offering wealth, penance, yogic disciplines, silent scriptural study, and knowledge.
Pranayama disciplines: pouring inhalation into exhalation and exhalation into inhalation to still breath.
Those who fast strictly offering life-breaths into life-breaths; all such offerings purge the taint of sin.
Partakers of the immortal sacrificial remnants attain eternal Brahman; without sacrifice neither world is won.
Diverse sacrifices spread before Brahman; recognizing them as products of action brings liberation.
The sacrifice of wisdom is superior to material oblations, for all action finds its consummation in knowledge.
Approach the seers of truth with reverence, earnest inquiry, and humble service to receive divine instruction.
Endowed with truth, you will never fall back into delusion, beholding all creatures in the Self and in Me.
Even the greatest sinner can cross over all ocean of transgression upon the reliable bark of spiritual wisdom.
As blazing flame reduces fuel to ashes, so the fire of knowledge (jñānāgniḥ) burns all works to ash.
No purifier exists comparable to wisdom; the person perfected in Yoga realizes it naturally within in due time.
The person endowed with faith, dedication, and sensory mastery secures knowledge and swiftly wins supreme peace.
The ignorant, faithless, and doubt-ridden soul is ruined; neither this world, nor heaven, nor joy awaits the doubter.
Actions cannot bind one who has renounced works through Yoga, severed doubts by wisdom, and possesses the Self.
Concluding call: cleave the doubt born of ignorance with the sword of wisdom, take refuge in Yoga, and arise!
Arjuna opening query: contrast between renunciation of actions (sannyāsa) and practice of selfless action (yoga).
Krishna reply: both paths lead to liberation, but karma-yoga is superior to mere renunciation of work.
Definition of true sannyāsin: one who neither hates nor desires, untouched by dualities; note [FN#8].
Reconciliation of Sankhya and Yoga: the immature regard them as separate, but mastering one yields the fruit of both.
Identity of ultimate goal: the realm attained by Sankhyans is reached by Yogins; who sees them as one sees truly.
Difficulty of renunciation without karma-yoga; seamlessly combined with 5.7 in shared source span.
Attributes of the pure-hearted yogayukta whose self is one with all life; shared source span with 5.6.
Consciousness of the seer of truth: "I do nothing at all" while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, breathing, sleeping.
Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening and shutting eyes, knowing senses operate among sense-objects.
Offering deeds to Brahman without attachment: sin taints him no more than water adheres to an enamelled lotus-leaf.
Yogins perform action solely with body, mind, intellect, and senses, shedding egoism for inner purification.
The disciplined seeker renouncing fruits gains steadfast peace; the selfish worker driven by desire is fettered.
The embodied soul mentally renouncing works rests serenely in the "city of nine gates" [FN#9], neither acting nor causing action.
The Sovereign of the world creates neither agency, nor action, nor karmic reward; Nature alone operates.
The Lord takes neither the good nor evil deeds of humans; spiritual darkness clouds knowledge, breeding delusion.
When ignorance is dispelled by Self-knowledge, that supreme wisdom shines like the rising sun.
Souls centered on That, merged in That, going to the state of no-return; includes bracketed poetic gloss.
Universal vision of the wise (samadarśinaḥ): seeing Brahman equally in scholar, cow, elephant, dog, and outcast.
Mortal world is conquered here on earth by minds established in equal vision, resting in sinless Brahman.
Neither overjoyed by pleasant fortune nor shaken by sorrow, steady of intellect, abiding untroubled in Brahman.
Detached from outward sensory impressions, one discovers bliss within; united with Brahman, he tastes eternal peace.
Sensual pleasures are but fertile wombs of grief with beginnings and endings; the wise mind finds no delight in them.
Blessed and happy is the person who masters the violent surge of lust and wrath here on earth before shedding the body.

Second group of knowledge attributes: contempt of sense pleasures (vairagya), self-sacrifice (anahankara), and perception of evil in birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering.

Announcement of that which is to be known (jneya) which grants immortality: the uncreated Para-Brahman, neither Sat nor Asat.
Classic cosmic vision of the Supreme having hands, feet, eyes, heads, mouths, and ears everywhere, encompassing the universe.
Faithful rendering of sarvendriyagunabhasa sarvendriyavivarjita: shining through all senses yet free from them, unattached yet sustaining all, master of modes yet attributeless.
Within and without all beings, unmoving yet moving, incomprehensible due to subtlety, both near and far.
Undivided yet seeming divided in all beings, sustainer of beings, devourer, and generator.
Light of lights beyond darkness, wisdom, the object of wisdom, seated in the hearts of all.
Summary of the field, knowledge, and the object of knowledge; the devotee who understands this attains Krishna's being.
Both Prakriti and Purusha are beginningless; all modifications and qualities originate from Prakriti.
Prakriti is the cause in the generation of causes and effects; Purusha is the cause in the experience of pleasure and pain.
Purusha dwelling in Prakriti experiences the Gunas, and attachment to the Gunas causes birth in good and evil wombs (yonis, annotated in note 29).
The Supreme Purusha in the body: spectator, permitter, supporter, experiencer, Great Lord, and Paramatman.
He who knows Purusha and Prakriti with the Gunas, in whatever state he lives, is not born again.
Diverse spiritual paths: some perceive the Self through meditation, others through Sankhya philosophy, others through Karma-yoga.
Those who lack direct knowledge but worship hearing from others also transcend death devoted to what they have heard.
Whatever being is born, moving or unmoving, arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field.
He who sees the Supreme Lord dwelling equally in all perishable beings as imperishable truly sees; cleanly begins at 'Know'.
Seeing the Lord equally present everywhere, he does not injure self by self and attains the supreme goal.
He who sees that all actions are performed solely by Prakriti and that the Self is non-agent truly sees.
When one sees the diversified existence of beings rooted in the One and expanding from It, he attains Brahman.
Being beginningless and attributeless, the Supreme Imperishable Self, even while dwelling in the body, neither acts nor is stained.
As all-pervading space is not tainted due to its subtlety, so the Self situated everywhere in the body is untainted.
As the single sun illuminates the whole world, so the Knower of the Field illuminates the entire field; bracketed gloss retained from source.
Those who perceive with the eye of wisdom the distinction between field and knower and the liberation of beings from Prakriti go to the Supreme.
Krishna declares supreme knowledge by knowing which all sages attained perfection.
Taking refuge in this wisdom, sages attain My nature, neither reborn at creation nor perturbed at dissolution.
Great Brahma (Prakriti) is My womb in which I place the seed, whence comes the birth of all beings.
In whatever wombs forms are produced, great Brahma is the womb and I am the seed-giving father.
Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas born of Prakriti bind the imperishable embodied soul in the body.
Sattva, being stainless, luminous, and healthy, binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge.
Rajas, passionate by nature, born of thirst and attachment, binds the embodied soul by attachment to actions.
Tamas, born of ignorance, deluding all embodied beings, binds by heedlessness, indolence, and sleep.
Sattva attaches to happiness, Rajas to action, while Tamas, shrouding wisdom, attaches to heedlessness/sloth.
Sattva prevails overpowering Rajas and Tamas; Rajas prevails overpowering Sattva and Tamas; Tamas prevails overpowering Sattva and Rajas.
When the light of knowledge shines through all gates of the body, Sattva is known to be predominant.
Greed, activity, undertaking of works, restlessness, and longing arise when Rajas is predominant; cleanly ends at 'engrained;'.
Darkness, stagnation, heedlessness, and delusion arise when Tamas is predominant; begins cleanly at 'and where'.
If the embodied soul meets death when Sattva prevails, it attains the stainless worlds of the knowers of the highest.
Dying in Rajas, one is born among those attached to work; dying in Tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded/witless.
The fruit of good action is Sattvic and pure; fruit of Rajas is pain; fruit of Tamas is ignorance/darkness.
From Sattva arises knowledge; from Rajas greed; from Tamas heedlessness, delusion, and ignorance.
Those established in Sattva rise upward; the Rajasic stay in the middle; the Tamasic sink downward into lowest conditions.
When the seer beholds no agent other than the Gunas and knows That which is beyond the Gunas, he attains My being.
Transcending the three Gunas that produce the body, the embodied soul is freed from birth, death, old age, and sorrow, drinking Amrit.
Arjuna asks the marks of one who has transcended the three Gunas, his conduct, and how he goes beyond them.
Krishna defines the Gunatita: he neither hates light, activity, or delusion when present, nor longs for them when absent.
Seated like an unconcerned witness, unperturbed by Gunas, knowing 'the Gunas operate', he stands firm and wavers not.
Equal in pain and pleasure, dwelling in the Self, regarding clod, stone, and gold alike, equal to pleasant and unpleasant, steadfast, equal in blame and praise; ends cleanly at 'dispraise;'.
Equal in honor and dishonor, equal to friend and foe, renouncing all enterprise—he is called transcender of Gunas; starts cleanly at 'satisfied'.
He who serves Me with unswerving Bhakti-yoga, transcending these Gunas, is fit for becoming Brahman.
For I am the abode of Brahman, of immortal and immutable life, of eternal Dharma, and of absolute bliss.
The inverted Ashvattha tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are Vedic hymns; he who knows it is the Veda-knower.
Its branches spread above and below nourished by Gunas with sense objects as buds; secondary roots stretch downward binding man to action; includes footnote 30.
Its true form is not perceived here, nor its end, beginning, or foundation; cutting down this firmly rooted Ashvattha with the strong weapon of detachment; ends at '--to set'.
Then that goal must be sought from which none return: 'I take refuge in that Primal Person whence streamed forth ancient cosmic activity'; starts at 'New growths'.
Free from pride and delusion, victorious over the evil of attachment, constant in spiritual knowledge, freed from dualities of pleasure and pain, the undeluded reach the eternal goal.
Neither sun, nor moon, nor fire illumines that supreme abode of Mine, having reached which souls do not return.
An eternal fraction of Myself in the world of the living, becoming a living soul, draws to itself the five senses and mind seated in Prakriti.
When the Lord acquires a body and when He leaves it, He takes these senses and mind along as the wind carries scents from flower-beds.
Presiding over ear, eye, touch, taste, smell, and mind, the soul experiences the objects of the senses.
The deluded do not perceive the soul departing, staying, or experiencing united with the Gunas; those with eyes of wisdom see.
Striving yogis perceive Him established in themselves; but the unrefined and unintelligent, though striving, do not perceive Him.
The radiance in the sun illuminating the entire universe, in the moon, and in fire—know that splendor to be Mine.
Entering the earth I sustain all beings with My vital force, and becoming the sapful moon I nourish all plants.
Becoming the Vaishvanara digestive fire in living bodies, uniting with prana and apana, I digest the four kinds of food; ends with note 31 marker.
Verified source omission. Arnold explicitly omits canonical 15.15 ('sarvasya cāhaṃ hṛdi sanniviṣṭo...'), confirmed by footnote 31 ('I omit a verse here, evidently interpolated.').
Two persons in the world: the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable (the immutable/kutastha).
The Supreme Person is another, declared as Paramatman, the imperishable Lord Who enters the three worlds and sustains them.
Since I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and the Vedas as Purushottama.
He who, undeluded, knows Me thus as the Purushottama, knows all and worships Me with his whole being.
Thus this most secret doctrine has been imparted by Me; knowing this, a man becomes truly wise and fulfills all duties.
Opening divine qualities: fearlessness, purity of heart, steadfastness in knowledge, charity, self-restraint, sacrifice, study, austerity, and uprightness; ends cleanly at 'Uprightness,'.
Continuation of divine qualities: harmlessness, truth, freedom from wrath, renunciation, peace, non-slander, compassion, uncovetousness, gentleness, modesty, steadiness; ends at 'grave,'.

Concluding divine qualities: vigour/radiance, forgiveness, fortitude, cleanliness, freedom from malice and excessive pride, characterizing one born to divine destiny; starts at 'with manhood nobly mixed'.
Demonic qualities: hypocrisy, pride, arrogance, wrath, harshness, and ignorance, belonging to one born of demonic destiny; includes footnote 32.
Divine endowment leads to liberation, demonic to bondage; Krishna reassures Arjuna that he is born with divine qualities.
Two orders of created beings in this world: the divine and the demonic; divine described at length, hear now of the demonic.
Demonic persons know neither right action nor renunciation; neither purity, right conduct, nor truth is found in them.
They say the world is without truth, without moral basis, without a Lord, brought about by sexual union alone, caused only by lust.
Holding this view, these ruined souls of small intellect and fierce deeds emerge as enemies of the world for its destruction.
Surrendering to insatiable desires, full of hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance, holding false notions through delusion, they act with unholy vows; ends cleanly at 'sinful course,'.
Beset with boundless anxieties ending only in death, regarding sensual enjoyment as the highest goal, convinced that this is all; starts cleanly at 'they trust this lie'.
Bound by hundreds of ties of hope, devoted to lust and anger, they strive by unjust means to accumulate wealth for sense gratification.
Inner monologue of the demonic: 'This has been gained by me today; this desire I shall obtain; this wealth is mine, and this also shall be mine in future'.
Demonic boasting: 'That enemy has been slain by me, and others also I shall slay; I am the lord, I enjoy, I am successful, powerful, and happy'.
Demonic self-glorification: 'I am wealthy and well-born; who else is equal to me? I will sacrifice, give alms, and rejoice', deluded by ignorance; ends at 'ignorance;'.
Bewildered by numerous thoughts, entangled in the mesh of delusion, addicted to gratification of lust, they fall into foul Naraka; starts at 'and so they fall--'.
Self-conceited, stubborn, filled with pride and intoxication of wealth, they perform ostentatious sacrifices in name only, disregarding scriptural injunctions.
Given over to egotism, power, insolence, lust, and wrath, these malicious people hate Me dwelling in their own bodies and those of others; ends at 'my foemen are,'.
Those who hate, cruel, evil, lowest of men—I cast them perpetually into demonic wombs in the cycle of samsara; ends at 'devilish womb,'.
Fallen into demonic wombs, deluded birth after birth, failing to reach Me, they sink to the lowest degradation; starts at 'whence--birth by birth--'.
Threefold is the gate of hell leading to self-ruin: lust, anger, and greed; therefore let a man renounce these three.
The man who is released from these three gates of darkness acts for his own welfare and thereby reaches the supreme goal.

Arjuna asks concerning those who worship with faith while disregarding scriptural ordinance: is their condition Sattva, Rajas, or Tamas?
Krishna replies that the faith of embodied beings is threefold according to their nature: Sattvic, Rajasic, and Tamasic.
The faith of each man conforms to his natural disposition; man is of the nature of his faith, whatever his faith is, that he is.
Sattvic men worship the gods; Rajasic men worship Yakshas and Rakshasas (note 34); Tamasic men worship ghosts (Pretas) and elemental spirits (Bhutas, note 35).
Men who practice severe austerities not enjoined by scripture, driven by hypocrisy and egoism, impelled by lust, attachment, and force; ends at 'violent, wild,'.
Senselessly torturing the elements within their body and Me residing within the body—know them to be of demonic resolve; starts at 'Torturing--the witless ones'.
Food also dear to each is threefold, as are sacrifices, austerities, and gifts; hear their distinctions.
Foods promoting longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy, which are savory, succulent, substantial, and agreeable, are dear to the Sattvic.
Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning, producing pain, grief, and disease, are dear to the Rajasic.
Food cooked more than three hours prior (yatayama, note 36), tasteless, putrid, stale, leftover, and impure, is dear to the Tamasic.
Sacrifice offered according to scriptural rule by men without desire for reward, with mind fixed that it ought to be done, is Sattvic.
Sacrifice performed seeking fruit or for the sake of ostentation—know that to be Rajasic, O best of Bharatas.
Sacrifice devoid of scriptural ordinance, distributing no food, without sacred mantras, without gifts to priests, and empty of faith, is Tamasic.
Austerity of the body: worship of gods, twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, uprightness, celibacy, and non-injury.
Austerity of speech: words causing no agitation, truthful, pleasant, beneficial, and the regular recitation of Vedic scriptures.
Austerity of mind: serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-control, and purity of feelings.
This threefold austerity practiced with supreme faith by steadfast men seeking no fruit is declared Sattvic.
Austerity practiced with hypocrisy for the sake of gaining welcome, honor, and reverence is declared Rajasic, unstable and fleeting.
Austerity performed through deluded obstinacy with self-torture or to cause harm to another is declared Tamasic.
Gift given as duty to one who cannot return it, in appropriate place, at proper time, and to a worthy recipient, is Sattvic.
Gift given with an expectation of return, or looking for fruit, or given grudgingly/with pain, is declared Rajasic.
Gift given at an inappropriate time or place, to unworthy persons, without respect or with contempt, is Tamasic; ends with footnote 37 marker.

Arjuna asks to understand distinctly the truth of Sannyasa and Tyaga, addressing Krishna as Mahabahu, Hrishikesha, and Keshinisudana.
Krishna defines Sannyasa as renunciation of desire-prompted actions and Tyaga as relinquishment of the fruits of all actions.
Some thinkers assert all action should be abandoned as defective, while others maintain sacrifice, gift, and austerity must not be abandoned.
Krishna gives His definitive verdict: Tyaga is declared to be of three kinds, O tiger among men.
Acts of sacrifice, gift, and austerity must not be abandoned but performed, for they are purifiers of the wise.
Even these acts should be performed abandoning attachment and fruits; this is My firm and highest conviction.
Renunciation of obligatory duty is not proper; abandonment thereof through delusion is declared Tamasic.
Abandoning action merely because it is troublesome or from fear of bodily affliction is Rajasic tyaga, yielding no fruit of renunciation.
When prescribed duty is performed simply because it ought to be done, relinquishing attachment and fruit, that is Sattvic tyaga.
The renouncer imbued with Sattva, intelligent, with doubts dispelled, neither hates disagreeable work nor clings to agreeable work.
No embodied being can wholly abandon action, but he who renounces the fruit of action is truly called a renouncer.
Threefold is the fruit of action (unwelcome, welcome, and mixed) accruing after death to non-renouncers, but never to Sannyasins.
Krishna announces the five causal factors declared in Sankhya doctrine for the accomplishment of all actions.
The five factors: the locus/body (adhisthana), the agent (karta), the various instruments (karana), the diverse efforts (ceshta), and the presiding divine/destiny (daivam).
Whatever action man undertakes by body, speech, or mind, right or reverse, these five are its causes.
Such being the case, whoever sees the pure Self as the sole actor owing to uncultivated intellect does not truly see.
He whose state of mind is free from egoism and whose intellect is untainted, even though he slay these people, does not slay and is not bound.
Knowledge, object of knowledge, and knower form the threefold impulse to action; instrument, action, and agent form the threefold composite of action.
Knowledge, action, and agent are declared to be threefold according to the distinction of Gunas; hear of them as they are.
Sattvic knowledge: that by which one sees one imperishable existence in all beings, undivided in the divided.
Rajasic knowledge: that which sees distinct manifold entities of various kinds in all beings as separate.
Tamasic knowledge: that which clings to a single isolated effect as if it were the whole, irrational, without real objective, and narrow.
Sattvic action: ordained action performed without attachment, without love or hate, by one desiring no fruit.
Rajasic action: action performed with immense strain by one seeking desire or driven by egoism.
Tamasic action: action undertaken from delusion, heedless of consequences, loss, harm to others, and personal capacity.
Sattvic agent: free from attachment, free from egotism, endowed with firmness and enthusiasm, unchanged in success or failure.
Rajasic agent: passionate, coveting fruit of work, greedy, hurtful, impure, subject to elation and depression.
Tamasic agent: discordant, undisciplined, obstinate, deceitful, malicious, indolent, despondent, and procrastinating.
Krishna introduces the threefold division of intellect (buddhi) and steadfastness (dhriti) according to the Gunas.
Sattvic intellect: knows action and renunciation, what ought and ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and release.
Rajasic intellect: erroneously perceives dharma and adharma, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Tamasic intellect: shrouded in darkness, regards adharma as dharma and perceives all things upside down.
Sattvic steadfastness: unswerving fortitude whereby through yoga one controls the functions of mind, prana, and senses.
Rajasic steadfastness: that by which one clings obstinately to duty, desire, and wealth from attachment and desire for rewards.
Tamasic steadfastness: that by which a foolish person does not abandon sleep, fear, grief, despondency, and arrogance.
Krishna announces the threefold nature of pleasure; Sattvic pleasure in which one rejoices through long practice and terminates grief.
Sattvic pleasure: like poison at first, like nectar at last, born of the clarity of self-realization; cleanly begins at 'bitter at first'.
Rajasic pleasure: born of contact of senses with sense-objects, nectar-like at first, poison-like at last.
Tamasic pleasure: that which deludes the self at the beginning and in the sequel, arising from sleep, indolence, and error.
There is no entity on earth or among the gods in heaven that is free from these three Gunas born of Prakriti.
Duties of Brahmans, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras are distributed according to the Gunas born of their own natures.
Inborn Brahman duties: tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance, uprightness, knowledge, realization, and religious faith.
Inborn Kshatriya duties: heroism, majesty, fortitude, dexterity, not fleeing from battle, generosity, and lordly demeanor.
Inborn Vaishya duties: agriculture, cattle-rearing, and commerce; inborn Shudra duty: service.

Devoted to his own natural duty, each man attains perfection; hear how one devoted to svadharma wins perfection (note: witness database carries corrupted 5.10 text, but Arnold translation is perfectly faithful to 18.45).
By worshipping Him from Whom all beings arise and by Whom all this is pervaded through performance of own duty, man attains perfection.
Better is one's own duty though imperfect than the duty of another well performed; doing duty ordained by nature incurs no guilt.
One should not abandon inborn duty even though faulty; all enterprises are obscured by defect as fire is enveloped in smoke.
With unattached intellect everywhere, self-subdued, desires departed, one attains supreme perfection of actionlessness through renunciation.
Hear briefly how one who has attained perfection attains Brahman, the supreme culmination of wisdom.
Endowed with pure intellect, controlling the self with fortitude, turning away from sound and other sense objects, casting off love and hatred.
Dwelling in solitude, eating sparingly, subduing body, speech, and mind, constantly devoted to meditation, cultivating dispassion.
Freed from egotism, power, arrogance, desire, wrath, and possessiveness, selfless and peaceful, he is qualified to become Brahman.
Becoming Brahman, serene in soul, he neither grieves nor desires; regarding all beings equally, he attains supreme devotion to Me.
Through devotion he comes to know Me in truth, what and who I am, and having known Me in truth, he enters Me forthwith.
Continuously performing all actions taking shelter in Me, by My grace he attains the eternal, imperishable state.
Mentally dedicating all actions to Me, making Me thy supreme goal, taking refuge in Buddhi-yoga, constantly fix thy mind on Me.
Fixing thy mind on Me, thou shalt overcome all obstacles by My grace; but if through egotism thou wilt not listen, thou shalt perish.
If, taking refuge in egoism, thou thinkest 'I will not fight', vain is this thy resolve; thy nature will compel thee.
Bound by thy own duty born of nature, what through delusion thou wishest not to do, that thou shalt helplessly perform.
The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, causing them to revolve by His divine Maya as if mounted on a machine.
Fly unto Him for refuge with all thy being; by His grace shalt thou obtain supreme peace and the eternal realm.
Thus has wisdom more secret than secret been disclosed to thee by Me; reflect on it fully, and then act as thou choosest.
Hear again My supreme word, the most secret of all; thou art intensely dear to Me, therefore I will declare what is for thy welfare.
Fix thy mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, prostrate before Me; to Me alone shalt thou come; truly do I promise thee, for thou art dear to Me.
Renouncing all religious rites and duties, take refuge in Me alone; I will release thee from all sins, do not grieve.
This must never be spoken by thee to one devoid of austerity, to one without devotion, to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who carps at Me.
He who imparts this supreme secret to My devotees, offering supreme devotion to Me, shall without doubt come to Me.
There is none among men who does more pleasing service to Me than he, nor shall there be another on earth dearer to Me.
And he who studies this sacred dialogue of ours shall have worshipped Me with the sacrifice of knowledge; such is My conviction.
The man who listens with faith and free from malice shall also be liberated and attain the radiant worlds of the righteous.
Has this been heard by thee, O Partha, with concentrated mind? Has the delusion of thy ignorance been dispelled, O Dhananjaya?
Arjuna answers: My delusion is destroyed, memory is regained by Thy grace, O Achyuta; I stand firm with doubts dispelled; I will do Thy bidding.
Sanjaya concludes: Thus have I heard this wondrous, hair-stirring dialogue between Vasudeva and the great-souled Partha.
By the grace of Vyasa have I heard this supreme and secret Yoga directly from Krishna, the Lord of Yoga Himself, as He spoke it.
O King, repeatedly remembering this wondrous and holy dialogue of Keshava and Arjuna, I rejoice again and again; ends at 'gladness:'.
Remembering repeatedly that exceedingly wondrous form of Hari, great is my amazement, O King, and I rejoice again and again; ends at 'love and bliss.'.
Wherever is Krishna the Lord of Yoga, wherever is the archer Partha, there are assured fortune, victory, prosperity, and righteous policy; this is my conviction.
